title: Attach the stock report to each settlement — on availability, backward — and see what the wrong join invents
concepts: fake predictability from a wrong join

explain.prompt: A colleague joined the stocks on week_ending and found that “the latest stock surprise predicts tomorrow's WTI return, t = −4.4”. In 4–6 sentences with your numbers: why is that result an artefact, what does your join do differently, and what do the age of the matched report and the tolerance protect against?
rubric: Joined on week_ending, a report is attached from the Friday it describes, five days or more before its publication: on 929 of 1,510 days the join uses a report not yet published.

On the eve of each release (Tuesday), the wrong join already 'knows' the surprise that will be published the next day at 10:30, so it 'predicts' the release-day move: correlation −0.245, slope t = −4.4, R² 6 %. With the backward join on available_at the same test gives −0.077 (t = −1.35).
The fake signal is the price reaction to the release itself, relabelled as a forecast: a release-time mismatch creates a false lead-lag.

The correct join takes, for each 14:30 New York settlement (converted to UTC), the last report with available_at ≤ decision time; the assertion checks that no matched report is from the future — it would fail on the week_ending join.

age_days (5 to 14 days here; 13–14 after the 12-day publication delay of June 2022) shows how stale the information is; the 10-day tolerance leaves a value blank rather than silently using a report that is too old (27–28 June 2022, when the last published report was 12 days old).
A backward join on the right key is necessary, not sufficient: the value must also be the vintage known at that time (3.3), and the features built on it must pass a truncation test (3.4).
